title: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No physical system can compute beyond cellular automata and Turing machines

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: As a law of nature, no system that can actually be constructed in our universe can carry out explicit computations more sophisticated than those of universal systems such as cellular automata and Turing machines; imaginable hypercomputers (e.g. with infinite tables of results) cannot be built.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: no system can ever carry out explicit computations that are more sophisticated than those carried out by systems like cellular automata and Turing machines.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Content of the Principle” (from p. 719), p. 720. Scope: all physical systems in our universe, including computers and brains

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.39

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing theory and experiments can reject specific hypercomputer designs based on infinite precision, energy, or time. They cannot decisively prove the unrestricted physical Church-Turing thesis.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Specify hypercomputation models and identify their required physical resources, then compare those requirements with tested physical laws and bounds. A reproducible physical device computing a formally non-Turing-computable function would refute the claim; existing physics can exclude particular proposals.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No finite set of observations covers every constructible system in the universe.

Hypercomputation cannot be certified from finitely many input-output trials alone.

The inference depends on extrapolating physical laws to untested regimes.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For several established theories, including ordinary quantum and classical models under finite preparation and readout, simulability by a Turing machine is a published mathematical question and can be assessed now. That covers a restricted scope. Nothing now available surveys every system that could be built, so the law-of-nature reading remains only partly tested.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Interpret more sophisticated as deciding a non-recursive set by a physical process whose preparation and readout are finite. Confirm the claim for a physical theory if that theory has a Turing simulation; refute the claim by a laboratory procedure that answers a known undecidable problem. Idealized infinite tables that cannot be built do not count.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A universal negative about every constructible system is not confirmed by simulating the theories we already have.

Proposed hypercomputers often depend on unphysical infinities, so an apparent counterexample may not meet the claim's constructibility condition.
